concepts.title: Wave problems: read the equation and boundary conditions together
concepts.explain: The wave equation comes from “mass × acceleration = force.” A string’s transverse wave speed is $c=\sqrt{T/\rho}$; a rod’s longitudinal wave speed is $c=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$. A fixed end prescribes displacement. A free end prescribes stress or slope.
concepts.conditions: Small linear oscillations and a uniform material. Choose spatial eigenfunctions matching each boundary type.
concepts.proof: Set $u=XT$ and separate to obtain $X''+\lambda X=0$ and $T''+c^2\lambda T=0$. Two fixed ends give $X_n=\sin(n\pi x/l)$ and $\omega_n=cn\pi/l$. Project the initial displacement to obtain $A_n$. Project the initial velocity and divide by $\omega_n$ to obtain $B_n$.

example.question: A string fixed at both ends has initial displacement $\sin(\pi x/l)$ and zero initial velocity. Find its motion.
example.solution: Only the first mode is present: $u(x,t)=\sin(\pi x/l)\cos(c\pi t/l)$. It satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, both end conditions, and both initial conditions.

concepts.memory: Displacement supplies cosine-in-time terms; velocity supplies sine-in-time terms. Choose the boundary-compatible modes before finding coefficients.

concepts.title: D’Alembert’s formula and characteristics
concepts.explain: An infinite string’s displacement is the sum of waves traveling in opposite directions. Initial velocity contributes an integral over the region of influence, rather than simply velocity multiplied by t. A fixed-end half-line can be handled by odd extension.
concepts.conditions: For $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ on the full line, without forcing, φ is the initial displacement and v the initial velocity. A classical solution needs sufficient smoothness. On a half-line, use odd extension for a fixed end and even extension for an insulated/free end.
concepts.proof: With characteristic variables ξ=x−ct and η=x+ct, the equation becomes $u_{\xi\eta}=0$, so $u=F(\xi)+H(\eta)$. At t=0, $F+H=\varphi$ and $c(H\prime-F\prime)=v$. Integrate to find the two functions and add them, giving the displayed formula. Differentiating in t at t=0 directly verifies the initial velocity v.

example.question: On the full line, the initial displacement is zero and the initial velocity is a constant V. How does displacement change?
example.solution: $u=(2c)^{-1}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}V\,ds=Vt$. The motion is spatially uniform, so $u_{xx}=u_{tt}=0$, and the initial velocity is correct.

concepts.memory: Average the displacement at the two endpoints; integrate the velocity between them and divide by 2c.

concepts.title: Modal equations for forcing and resonance
concepts.explain: Once spatial boundary conditions are homogeneous, project the forcing and initial data onto the same eigenfunctions. Each mode is a forced oscillator. At resonance, the nonresonant formula has a zero denominator and must be replaced.
concepts.conditions: Use an orthogonal spatial eigenbasis with $\omega_n>0$ and $B_n=q_n\prime(0)/\omega_n$. A zero mode must separately solve $q_0\prime\prime=F_0$. Damping modifies the time equation.
concepts.proof: Insert the spatial expansion into the equation and use orthogonality to obtain the equations for qₙ. The kernel $\sin\omega_n(t-s)/\omega_n$ is zero at t=s and has t derivative 1 there. Differentiating the convolution twice therefore produces Fₙ(t), while both initial values of the convolution are zero.

example.question: With zero initial data, what is the resonant response of $q\prime\prime+\omega^2q=F\cos\omega t$?
example.solution: The convolution or undetermined coefficients gives $q=Ft\sin\omega t/(2\omega)$. Its envelope grows with t. Differentiating twice verifies both the forcing and the zero initial data.

concepts.memory: Project in space first, then solve the oscillator in time. A zero denominator means check resonance.

concepts.title: Transport problems: read the equation and boundary conditions together
concepts.explain: Heat conservation and Fourier’s law give the heat equation. Every nonzero spatial mode of the source-free heat equation decays exponentially. Insulated boundaries retain a zero mode; fixed zero-temperature boundaries do not.
concepts.conditions: The medium is uniform. $k$ is thermal conductivity and $\rho c$ is heat capacity per unit volume. The source $s$ has already been divided by that heat capacity.
concepts.proof: For a segment $dx$, the rate of increase of internal energy is $\rho cS u_tdx$. Net heat input through its ends is $kS[u_x(x+dx)-u_x(x)]$. Divide by $Sdx$ and take the limit: $\rho c u_t=ku_{xx}+q$. Separation gives $T'+\kappa\lambda T=0$, hence $T=e^{-\kappa\lambda t}$.

example.question: A rod held at zero temperature at both ends starts at $\sin(2\pi x/l)$. Find its temperature.
example.solution: $u=e^{-4\kappa\pi^2t/l^2}\sin(2\pi x/l)$. Two spatial derivatives contribute $-(2\pi/l)^2$, matching the time decay rate.

concepts.memory: The heat equation is first order in time and needs one initial condition. Higher spatial frequencies decay faster.

concepts.title: The heat kernel, image extension, and diffusion scale
concepts.explain: The infinite-domain heat kernel is a Gaussian that broadens with time. For a zero-temperature half-line boundary, subtract the reflected image. For an insulated boundary, add it. The diffusion scale grows as $\sqrt t$.
concepts.conditions: For $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$, κ>0 and t>0, on the source-free full line. Initial data are recovered at continuity points or in an appropriate Lᵖ sense. On the half-line, distinguish Dirichlet from Neumann boundaries first.
concepts.proof: The Fourier transform gives $\widehat u_t=-\kappa k^2\widehat u$, hence $\widehat u=e^{-\kappa k^2t}\widehat\varphi$. The inverse Gaussian transform gives K, and $\int Kdx=1$. Odd extension becomes $K(x-\xi)-K(x+\xi)$ on the half-line, canceling the value at x=0. Even extension uses a plus sign and cancels the derivative at x=0.

example.question: For a unit point pulse of initial temperature, does the total heat change with time?
example.solution: The temperature is K and its integral $\int Kdx=1$ stays constant. The peak decreases as $t^{-1/2}$, while the width increases as $\sqrt{\kappa t}$.

concepts.memory: The heat kernel has total mass 1. Subtract images for a zero value; add them for a zero derivative.

concepts.title: Make nonhomogeneous boundaries homogeneous first
concepts.explain: Direct separation of variables needs homogeneous boundaries. First choose a simple function h satisfying the prescribed boundary values, then set u=v+h. If the boundary changes with time, the equation for v usually acquires a new source.
concepts.conditions: For example, with $u(0,t)=A(t)$ and $u(L,t)=B(t)$, choose $h=A+(B-A)x/L$. The boundary values of v are zero, but its initial data must also have h(x,0) subtracted.
concepts.proof: Substitute u=v+h term by term and move the h terms to the right. Since h satisfies the original boundaries, v has homogeneous boundaries. A linear h for constant boundary values has $h_t=h_{xx}=0$ and adds no source. For time-dependent boundaries, retain $-h_t$; omitting it leaves a residual in the original equation.

example.question: A thin rod starts at zero temperature and its ends are held at 0 and T. What is its steady state?
example.solution: Take $h=Tx/L$. Then v=u−h has zero values at both ends and initial data −Tx/L. Expand v in sine modes, each of which decays. As t→∞, v→0, so u→Tx/L.

concepts.memory: Subtract the boundary function. Subtract it from the initial data too. Check whether the equation gains a source.

concepts.title: Steady fields: read the equation and boundaries together
concepts.explain: A steady field does not depend on time. A source-free steady field satisfies Laplace’s equation. On a rectangle, separation gives trigonometric functions in one direction and hyperbolic functions in the other. Project the nonzero boundary values to find coefficients.
concepts.conditions: A source-free rectangular region. Choose the orthogonal basis using the homogeneous boundaries, then satisfy the nonhomogeneous boundary.
concepts.proof: Substituting $u=XY$ into $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ gives $X''/X=-Y''/Y=-\lambda$. If the values at $x=0,a$ are zero, $\lambda=(n\pi/a)^2$ and $X=\sin(n\pi x/a)$. If the value at $y=0$ is also zero, choose $Y$ as $\sinh(n\pi y/a)$.

example.question: On a rectangle, the top edge has $u(x,b)=\sin(\pi x/a)$ and the other three edges have zero values.
example.solution: $u=\sin(\pi x/a)\sinh(\pi y/a)/\sinh(\pi b/a)$. It satisfies Laplace’s equation, all three zero edges, and the prescribed top edge.

concepts.memory: Use two homogeneous sides to choose the orthogonal basis, then a hyperbolic factor to reach the nonzero side.

concepts.title: Uniqueness and the maximum principle for Laplace’s equation
concepts.explain: Boundary values do more than fix coefficients: they determine whether the solution is unique. To compare results from two methods, study their difference.
concepts.conditions: A bounded connected domain, sufficiently regular harmonic functions, and Dirichlet boundaries. An exterior domain also requires behavior at infinity. A pure Neumann problem determines the solution only up to a constant and requires compatibility.
concepts.proof: The difference w of two solutions is harmonic with zero boundary values. Green’s first identity gives $\int_V|\nabla w|^2dV=\oint w\partial_nw-\int w\Delta w=0$. Thus w is constant; its zero boundary value makes it zero. The maximum principle also bounds w above and below by zero.

example.question: A sphere’s surface is held at temperature 5 and there is no internal heat source. Could the center be hotter?
example.solution: The constant function 5 satisfies the equation and the boundary. Uniqueness makes it the only solution. The maximum principle also prevents a steady interior value above the boundary maximum.

concepts.memory: Subtract two solutions. Zero energy implies a constant. Use the boundary to fix that constant.

concepts.title: Sturm–Liouville problems: read the equation and boundaries together
concepts.explain: The different series arising from different boundaries all come from self-adjoint eigenvalue problems. The weight function defines the projection inner product. Self-adjoint boundaries ensure real eigenvalues. Nonnegative eigenvalues additionally require a nonnegative energy quadratic form; the differential-equation coefficients alone do not guarantee this.
concepts.formula: (p y')'-q y+\lambda w y=0,\qquad\langle f,g\rangle_w=\int_a^b w f\overline g\,dx
concepts.conditions: In the regular case, $p>0,w>0$, $q$ is real, and separated real self-adjoint boundary conditions are imposed. Singular endpoints need additional finiteness or integrability conditions.
concepts.proof: Multiply the equation for $y_m$ by $\overline{y_n}$ and subtract the conjugate equation for $y_n$ multiplied by $y_m$. Integrating gives $(\lambda_m-\overline{\lambda_n})\int w y_m\overline{y_n}=-[p(y_m'\overline{y_n}-y_m\overline{y_n'})]_a^b$. Self-adjoint boundaries make the right side zero. Taking $m=n$ proves real eigenvalues. Taking distinct eigenvalues proves weighted orthogonality.

example.question: Write $xy''+(1-x)y'+ay=0$ in self-adjoint form.
example.solution: Multiply by $e^{-x}$ to obtain $(xe^{-x}y')'+ae^{-x}y=0$. Thus $p=xe^{-x}$, $q=0$, $w=e^{-x}$, and $\lambda=a$.

concepts.memory: First combine the derivative terms into $(p y')'$. Always include the weight when projecting.

exercises.title: Pluck and release a string at its quarter point
exercises.question: A uniform string has length $l$, linear density $\rho$, tension $T$, and fixed ends $x=0,l$. A small transverse force $F$ ($F\ll T$) pulls it at $x=l/4$ until it is at rest, then is released. (1) Formulate the complete problem. (2) Solve by separation of variables.
exercises.idea: First find the triangular initial displacement from static equilibrium, then expand it in the sine modes for two fixed ends.
exercises.hint: The displacement at the plucking point is $h=3Fl/(16T)$. Alternatively, $-T\varphi''=F\delta(x-l/4)$ quickly gives the coefficients.
exercises.solution:
1. The difference of transverse tension forces on a segment is $Tu_{xx}dx$, and its mass is $\rho dx$. Thus $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, with $c^2=T/\rho$.
2. The static string is straight on each side of the pull. With $a=l/4$ and height $h$, force balance gives $T[h/a+h/(l-a)]=F$, hence $h=3Fl/(16T)$. The initial displacement is $\varphi(x)=3Fx/(4T)$ for $0\le x\le l/4$ and $F(l-x)/(4T)$ for $l/4\le x\le l$. Initial velocity is zero.
3. The complete conditions are $u(0,t)=u(l,t)=0$, $u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$, and $u_t(x,0)=0$.
4. Choose $X_n=\sin k_nx$ with $k_n=n\pi/l$. Using the static corner equation or piecewise integration gives
$$A_n=\frac2l\int_0^l\varphi(x)\sin k_nx\,dx=\frac{2Fl}{Tn^2\pi^2}\sin\frac{n\pi}4.$$
Therefore
$$u(x,t)=\frac{2Fl}{T\pi^2}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\sin(n\pi/4)}{n^2}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}\cos\frac{cn\pi t}{l}.$$
Tension has units N and linear density kg/m, so $c$ indeed has units m/s.
exercises.answer: $u_{tt}=(T/\rho)u_{xx}$, zero displacement at both ends, the triangular initial displacement above, and zero initial velocity. $u=\frac{2Fl}{T\pi^2}\sum_{n\ge1}\sin(n\pi/4)\sin(n\pi x/l)\cos(cn\pi t/l)/n^2$.
exercises.pattern: Static pull → slope-jump balance gives the triangular initial shape → sine projection → zero initial velocity retains only cosine-in-time terms.
exercises.pitfall: $F$ acts before release. After release the equation has zero forcing; do not keep a sustained force in it.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Release a compressed rod with one fixed end
exercises.question: A uniform slender rod has length $l$, cross-section $S$, mass density $\rho$, and Young’s modulus $Y$. The end $x=0$ is fixed. Compress it from $x=l$ to length $l(1-2e)$, bring it to rest, and release it. (1) Formulate its longitudinal-vibration problem. (2) Solve by separation.
exercises.idea: Measure displacement from the undeformed rod. The fixed end has zero displacement; the released end has zero stress.
exercises.hint: Uniform initial compression gives $u(x,0)=-2ex$. The fixed–free basis consists of half-integer sine modes.
exercises.solution:
1. The axial force is $N=YSu_x$. Force balance gives $\rho S u_{tt}=(YSu_x)_x$, so $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ and $c=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$.
2. After release, $u(0,t)=0,u_x(l,t)=0$. The uniform strain $-2e$ gives $u(x,0)=-2ex,u_t(x,0)=0$.
3. The eigenfunctions are $\sin k_nx$, where $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$, $n=0,1,\ldots$. Their squared norm is $l/2$, so
$$A_n=-\frac{4e}l\int_0^l x\sin k_nx\,dx=-\frac{4e(-1)^n}{lk_n^2}.$$
4. Thus
$$u(x,t)=-\frac{4e}l\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{k_n^2}\sin k_nx\cos(ck_nt).$$
The initial strain is not zero at the free end: this reflects the instantaneous removal of the applied force. Interpret the solution in an energy sense or by interior limits. The released-end stress condition holds for $t>0$.
exercises.answer: $u_{tt}=(Y/\rho)u_{xx}$; $u(0,t)=0,u_x(l,t)=0$; initial displacement $-2ex$, zero initial velocity, and the half-integer sine series above.
exercises.pattern: Longitudinal rod vibration → Young’s stress → distinguish fixed and free ends → half-integer frequencies → project the initial deformation.
exercises.pitfall: The released end has zero stress, not zero displacement. Cross-sectional area cancels from the wave speed.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Release a compressed rod with both ends free
exercises.question: A uniform slender rod has length $l$, cross-section $S$, density $\rho$, and Young’s modulus $Y$. Compress it from both ends to length $l(1-2e)$, bring it to rest, and release both ends simultaneously. (1) Formulate the problem. (2) Solve by separation of variables.
exercises.idea: Both released ends have zero stress. Choose symmetric compression with the center fixed to specify the initial displacement. The constant mode represents rigid translation.
exercises.hint: Take $u(x,0)=e(l-2x)$. Its cosine expansion contains only odd modes.
exercises.solution:
The uniform rod satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $c=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$ and $u_x(0,t)=u_x(l,t)=0$. For symmetric compression with the center unmoved, $u(x,0)=e(l-2x)$ and $u_t(x,0)=0$. The length change is indeed $u(l,0)-u(0,0)=-2el$.
The Neumann basis contains a constant and $\cos(n\pi x/l)$. The initial displacement has zero mean, so the constant mode is not excited. For $n\ge1$,
$$A_n=\frac2l\int_0^l e(l-2x)\cos\frac{n\pi x}l dx=\frac{4el[1-(-1)^n]}{n^2\pi^2}.$$
Thus
$$u=\frac{8el}{\pi^2}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\cos[(2m+1)\pi x/l]\cos[c(2m+1)\pi t/l]}{(2m+1)^2}.$$
If the compression process specifies only the final length, rather than the center position, an arbitrary constant $C$ may be added to the initial displacement and the solution. This changes only rigid translation, not deformation or vibration. Treat the instantaneous mismatch between initial endpoint strain and the released-end condition in the energy-solution sense.
exercises.answer: Both ends have $u_x=0$. With the fixed-center convention, the initial displacement is $e(l-2x)$ and velocity zero. $u=\frac{8el}{\pi^2}\sum_{m\ge0}\cos[(2m+1)\pi x/l]\cos[c(2m+1)\pi t/l]/(2m+1)^2$, up to an arbitrary constant translation.
exercises.pattern: Free–free rod → cosine basis including a zero mode → fix the center or mean first → project to find the symmetry-selected modes.
exercises.pitfall: The compressed length alone does not determine rigid translation. Do not omit the zero-frequency rigid mode.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: The damped-string equation
exercises.question: A uniform string oscillates transversely in a damping medium. The resistance per unit length is $f=-Ru_t$. Its linear density is $\rho$ and tension is $T$. Derive the vibration equation.
exercises.idea: Include both the tension difference and distributed resistance in the force balance of a short segment.
exercises.hint: Inertia per unit length is $\rho u_{tt}$.
exercises.solution:
For a segment $dx$, the difference of vertical tension components is $T[u_x(x+dx)-u_x(x)]\approx Tu_{xx}dx$. Resistance is $-Ru_tdx$. Newton’s law gives $\rho dx\,u_{tt}=Tu_{xx}dx-Ru_tdx$. Therefore
$$\rho u_{tt}+Ru_t-Tu_{xx}=0,$$
or $u_{tt}+2\gamma u_t=c^2u_{xx}$, where $2\gamma=R/\rho$ and $c^2=T/\rho$. For fixed or zero-flux boundaries, $dE/dt=-R\int u_t^2dx\le0$. This confirms the positive sign of the damping term on the left.
exercises.answer: $u_{tt}+(R/\rho)u_t=(T/\rho)u_{xx}$.
exercises.pattern: Segment force balance → consistent per-unit-length terms → resistance opposes velocity → verify the sign using energy decay.
exercises.pitfall: Writing $u_{tt}-(R/\rho)u_t=c^2u_{xx}$ would make energy grow, so that sign is wrong.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A Robin condition for a spring at a rod end
exercises.question: A uniform rod has length $l$, cross-section $S$, density $\rho$, and Young’s modulus $Y$. Its end $x=0$ is fixed. Its end $x=l$ is attached to a light spring of stiffness $k$, with the spring’s other end fixed and its equilibrium length unstretched. Compress the rod from the right to length $l(1-2e)$, bring it to rest, and release it. (1) Formulate the problem. (2) Solve by separation.
exercises.idea: Balance rod stress against the spring’s restoring force at the right end to get a Robin boundary and a transcendental eigenvalue equation.
exercises.hint: Set $h=k/(YS)$. The positive roots satisfy $\mu\cos\mu l+h\sin\mu l=0$.
exercises.solution:
Inside the rod, $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $c^2=Y/\rho$. The left end has $u(0,t)=0$. There is no concentrated mass at the right end, so force balance gives $YSu_x(l,t)=-ku(l,t)$, or $u_x(l,t)+hu(l,t)=0$.
The initial displacement is $-2ex$ and initial velocity is zero. Separation gives $X_n=\sin\mu_nx$, where $\mu_n>0$ solves $\mu_n\cos(\mu_nl)+h\sin(\mu_nl)=0$. The squared norm is
$$N_n=\int_0^l\sin^2\mu_nx\,dx=\frac l2-\frac{\sin2\mu_nl}{4\mu_n}.$$
The projection coefficients are
$$A_n=\frac{-2e[-l\cos(\mu_nl)/\mu_n+\sin(\mu_nl)/\mu_n^2]}{N_n}=-\frac{2e(1+hl)\sin(\mu_nl)}{\mu_n^2N_n}.$$
Finally, $u(x,t)=\sum_nA_n\sin\mu_nx\cos(c\mu_nt)$. For $k=0$, this reduces to the fixed–free rod. As $k\to\infty$, it approaches fixed–fixed boundaries. Both limits check the condition.
exercises.answer: $u_{tt}=(Y/\rho)u_{xx}$, $u(0,t)=0$, and $YSu_x(l,t)+ku(l,t)=0$. $u=\sum_nA_n\sin\mu_nx\cos(c\mu_nt)$, with $A_n,N_n,\mu_n$ as above.
exercises.pattern: End spring → force balance gives a Robin condition → solve the transcendental spectrum equation → project using the actual squared norm.
exercises.pitfall: A spring end is neither simply fixed nor simply free. Noninteger-frequency sine functions generally do not have squared norm $l/2$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Variable tension in a hanging heavy rope
exercises.question: A flexible rope of length $l$ and uniform density $\rho$ hangs from a fixed end with its other end free. Derive its small transverse-vibration equation about equilibrium.
exercises.idea: Tension is the weight of the rope below the chosen point, so it varies with position and must stay inside the spatial derivative.
exercises.hint: Measure $x$ downward from the upper end. Then $T(x)=\rho g(l-x)$, with $\rho$ interpreted as linear density.
exercises.solution:
Take $x\in[0,l]$ downward from the top and $u$ as the small horizontal displacement. Equilibrium tension equals the weight below: $T(x)=\rho g(l-x)$. Transverse force balance is
$$\rho u_{tt}=\partial_x[T(x)u_x].$$
Substitution gives
$$u_{tt}=g[(l-x)u_{xx}-u_x].$$
The top is fixed, $u(0,t)=0$. At the lower end, the natural condition is $\lim_{x\to l^-}T(x)u_x(x,t)=0$, with finite displacement. Since $T(l)=0$ makes this endpoint singular, do not impose the extra condition $u_x(l,t)=0$. With upward coordinate $s=l-x$ from the lower end, the equation becomes $u_{tt}=g(su_{ss}+u_s)$. No initial data are supplied; the question asks only for the equation.
exercises.answer: With x measured downward from the top, $u_{tt}=g\partial_x[(l-x)u_x]=g[(l-x)u_{xx}-u_x]$.
exercises.pattern: Heavy rope → use the lower segment’s weight to find equilibrium tension → retain $(Tu_x)_x$ → specify the coordinate direction and natural endpoint condition.
exercises.pitfall: Variable tension requires $(Tu_x)_x$. Omitting $T'u_x$ loses a term.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A rotating light rope: specify the transverse direction
exercises.question: A flexible light rope has length $l$ and uniform density $\rho$. One end is fixed to a vertical rotating axis and the other is free. The axis rotates the rope with angular speed $\omega$. Derive the small transverse-vibration equation about the equilibrium horizontal line.
exercises.idea: Use the outer segment’s centripetal force to find tension, then specify whether the motion is vertical or within the rotating plane. The question does not state the direction, and the two models differ.
exercises.hint: Measure $x$ outward from the axis. Then $T(x)=\int_x^l\rho\omega^2s\,ds=\rho\omega^2(l^2-x^2)/2$.
exercises.solution:
Neglect gravity and stretching. Measure $x$ outward from the axis, with the equilibrium rope straight along a horizontal radius. The outer segment’s required centripetal force gives
$$T(x)=\frac{\rho\omega^2}{2}(l^2-x^2).$$
If $u$ is a small vertical displacement out of the horizontal plane, as in the usual vertical transverse-vibration model, vertical inertia has no centrifugal term. Thus
$$u_{tt}=\frac1\rho(Tu_x)_x=\frac{\omega^2}{2}[(l^2-x^2)u_{xx}-2xu_x].$$
If instead $u$ is a small in-plane displacement perpendicular to the original rope, measured in coordinates rotating with the axis, the transverse inertial acceleration is $u_{tt}-\omega^2u$ (the first-order radial displacement is zero and the tension perturbation satisfies radial balance). Then
$$u_{tt}=\frac{\omega^2}{2}[(l^2-x^2)u_{xx}-2xu_x]+\omega^2u.$$
Both models have $u(0,t)=0$ and a free-end condition $Tu_x\to0$ with finite displacement. Since the question does not specify the vibration plane, state the directional assumption along with the answer. Do not switch between these equations without explanation.
exercises.answer: The equilibrium tension is $T=\rho\omega^2(l^2-x^2)/2$. For vertical transverse motion, $u_{tt}=(\omega^2/2)[(l^2-x^2)u_{xx}-2xu_x]$. For relative transverse motion within the rotating plane, add $\omega^2u$ to the right side.
exercises.pattern: Rotating rope → integrate outer-segment centripetal force → specify frame and vibration direction → combine tension divergence and inertia.
exercises.pitfall: The direction is ambiguous. Do not add a horizontal centrifugal term to vertical motion, or omit it from relative in-plane motion.
exercises.verification: Independent Newtonian modeling with the vibration plane explicitly stated because the question leaves it unspecified. No unread teacher answer is used as verification.

exercises.title: Matching conditions at a point mass on a string
exercises.question: A uniform flexible string of length $l$ is fixed at both ends and carries a mass $m$ at an interior point $x_0$. Find the matching conditions there during small transverse motion.
exercises.idea: Displacement is continuous at the attached mass. The difference of transverse tension forces supplies its inertia.
exercises.hint: Integrate the momentum equation across the point mass and define the slope jump consistently.
exercises.solution:
The string stays attached to the mass, so
$$u(x_0^-,t)=u(x_0^+,t)=:u_0(t).$$
For the mass, the right string exerts transverse force $Tu_x(x_0^+,t)$ and the left exerts $-Tu_x(x_0^-,t)$. Thus
$$T[u_x(x_0^+,t)-u_x(x_0^-,t)]=m u_0''(t).$$
If gravity is present, define $u$ relative to the sagging static equilibrium. Static weight is already balanced by static tension; the relations above describe the linear perturbation. Each side still satisfies $\rho u_{tt}=Tu_{xx}$, and the endpoints are fixed.
exercises.answer: $[u]_{x_0}=0$ and $T[u_x]_{x_0}=m u_{tt}(x_0,t)$, where jump means right minus left.
exercises.pattern: Concentrated component → continuous displacement → momentum balance across the point → replace ordinary slope continuity by an inertia relation.
exercises.pitfall: With a point mass, $u_x$ is generally discontinuous. Do not simply set the left and right slopes equal.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A finite-width hammer strike on a string
exercises.question: A uniform string of length $l$ and linear density $\rho$, fixed at both ends, starts in equilibrium. A hammer of width $2\delta$ instantaneously strikes $[x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta]$, giving total impulse $I$. (1) Formulate the problem. (2) Find the motion by separation.
exercises.idea: Impulse determines initial velocity, not displacement. Total impulse and width alone do not determine its spatial distribution. Use the usual uniform-strike assumption and also state the general formula.
exercises.hint: Uniform impulse density is $j=I/(2\delta)$. Initial velocity is $v=j/\rho$, and initial displacement is zero.
exercises.solution:
Assume the struck interval lies wholly inside $(0,l)$ and the impulse acts in one transverse direction. In general, $u_t(x,0)=j(x)/\rho$ with $\int_0^l j(x)dx=I$. The total $I$ alone does not uniquely determine $j$.
For the usual uniform hammer-face model, $j(x)=I/(2\delta)$ on the struck interval and zero elsewhere. The complete problem is $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $c^2=T/\rho$, $u(0,t)=u(l,t)=0$, $u(x,0)=0$, and the velocity just specified.
Let $k_n=n\pi/l$ and $\Omega_n=ck_n$. The velocity coefficients are
$$V_n=\frac2{\rho l}\int j(x)\sin k_nx\,dx=\frac{2I\sin(k_nx_0)\sin(k_n\delta)}{\rho l\delta k_n}.$$
Therefore
$$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2I\sin(k_nx_0)\sin(k_n\delta)}{\rho l\delta c k_n^2}\sin k_nx\sin\Omega_nt.$$
For any other impulse distribution, use $V_n=2(\rho l)^{-1}\int j\sin k_nx$ instead. As $\delta\to0$, the displacement coefficient tends to $2I\sin(k_nx_0)/(\rho lc k_n)$, agreeing with a point impulse.
exercises.answer: With uniform impulse, $u=\sum_{n\ge1}2I\sin(k_nx_0)\sin(k_n\delta)\sin k_nx\sin(ck_nt)/(\rho l\delta c k_n^2)$, $k_n=n\pi/l$.
exercises.pattern: Instantaneous impulse → $\rho v=j$ → sine-project velocity → divide by modal frequency → check the point-impulse limit.
exercises.pitfall: The initial velocity amplitude is $I/(2\delta\rho)$, not the total impulse $I$. State the uniform-distribution assumption.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A double-sine solution for a square membrane
exercises.question: A uniform square membrane of side $a$ is fixed on all four edges. Its initial displacement is $\varphi(x,y)$ and initial velocity $v(x,y)$. Find its two-dimensional transverse motion.
exercises.idea: Use a double-sine basis for the four fixed edges. Each pair of positive integers has one natural frequency.
exercises.hint: $\Omega_{mn}=c\pi\sqrt{m^2+n^2}/a$.
exercises.solution:
Let $\tau$ be tension per unit length and $\sigma$ the areal density, so $c^2=\tau/\sigma$. The membrane satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2(u_{xx}+u_{yy})$ for $0<x,y<a$, with $u=0$ on all four edges. Write
$$u=\sum_{m,n\ge1}[A_{mn}\cos\Omega_{mn}t+B_{mn}\sin\Omega_{mn}t]\sin\frac{m\pi x}a\sin\frac{n\pi y}a,$$
where $\Omega_{mn}=(c\pi/a)\sqrt{m^2+n^2}$. Double orthogonality gives
$$A_{mn}=\frac4{a^2}\int_0^a\int_0^a\varphi(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}a\sin\frac{n\pi y}a\,dxdy,$$
$$B_{mn}=\frac4{a^2\Omega_{mn}}\int_0^a\int_0^a v(x,y)\sin\frac{m\pi x}a\sin\frac{n\pi y}a\,dxdy.$$
The two spatial second derivatives contribute $-\pi^2(m^2+n^2)/a^2$, verifying the frequency. A classical solution also requires initial data compatible with the fixed boundaries.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum_{m,n\ge1}[A_{mn}\cos\Omega_{mn}t+B_{mn}\sin\Omega_{mn}t]\sin(m\pi x/a)\sin(n\pi y/a)$, with the double-projection coefficients above.
exercises.pattern: Separate in two dimensions → add the two spatial eigenvalues → double orthogonal projection → divide the velocity coefficient by frequency.
exercises.pitfall: The double-projection factor is $4/a^2$. Frequency depends on $\sqrt{m^2+n^2}$, not $m+n$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A forced string with one spatial mode
exercises.question: A uniform string of length $l$, fixed at both ends, experiences a sustained force per unit length $f(x,t)=A\sin(2\pi x/l)\sin\omega t$. Starting at rest in equilibrium, find its forced motion.
exercises.idea: The forcing excites only the second spatial mode, reducing the problem to one forced oscillator.
exercises.hint: Set $u=q(t)\sin(2\pi x/l)$. Then $q''+\Omega^2q=(A/\rho)\sin\omega t$, $\Omega=2\pi c/l$.
exercises.solution:
The string equation is $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=f/\rho$, with $c^2=T/\rho$. The single-mode ansatz gives $q''+\Omega^2q=(A/\rho)\sin\omega t$, $q(0)=q'(0)=0$.
For nonresonance, $\omega\ne\Omega$, take the particular solution $A\sin\omega t/[\rho(\Omega^2-\omega^2)]$ and add a homogeneous term to satisfy the initial data:
$$q=\frac{A}{\rho(\Omega^2-\omega^2)}\left(\sin\omega t-\frac\omega\Omega\sin\Omega t\right).$$
At resonance, $\omega=\Omega>0$, use a limit or convolution:
$$q=\frac{A}{2\rho\Omega^2}(\sin\Omega t-\Omega t\cos\Omega t).$$
The answer is $u=q(t)\sin(2\pi x/l)$. The added term makes $q'(0)=0$, and the resonant solution contains linear growth in time.
exercises.answer: $u=q\sin(2\pi x/l)$. Off resonance, $q=A[\sin\omega t-(\omega/\Omega)\sin\Omega t]/[\rho(\Omega^2-\omega^2)]$. At resonance, $q=A(\sin\Omega t-\Omega t\cos\Omega t)/(2\rho\Omega^2)$.
exercises.pattern: A single spatial eigenfunction in the force → one modal ODE → particular solution plus transient → treat resonance separately.
exercises.pitfall: The steady $\sin\omega t$ term alone does not meet zero initial velocity. At resonance, do not divide by zero.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A fixed-end string driven by a point force
exercises.question: A uniform string of length $l$ is fixed at both ends. A sustained transverse force $f(t)=A\sin\omega t$ acts at $x_0$. Starting at rest in equilibrium, find the forced motion.
exercises.idea: Represent the point force by a delta distribution. Projection gives one forced oscillator for every spatial mode.
exercises.hint: For index $n$, the modal force amplitude is $F_n=2A\sin(n\pi x_0/l)/(\rho l)$.
exercises.solution:
The equation is $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=A\delta(x-x_0)\sin\omega t/\rho$, with zero endpoint values and zero displacement and velocity initially. Set $k_n=n\pi/l,\Omega_n=ck_n$, and $u=\sum q_n\sin k_nx$. Projection gives
$$q_n''+\Omega_n^2q_n=F_n\sin\omega t,\quad F_n=\frac{2A}{\rho l}\sin k_nx_0.$$
For $\omega\ne\Omega_n$,
$$q_n=\frac{F_n}{\Omega_n^2-\omega^2}\left(\sin\omega t-\frac\omega{\Omega_n}\sin\Omega_nt\right).$$
If $\omega=\Omega_N$, replace the $N$th term by $q_N=F_N[\sin\Omega_Nt-\Omega_Nt\cos\Omega_Nt]/(2\Omega_N^2)$ and keep the other terms nonresonant. If $\sin k_Nx_0=0$, that resonant mode is not driven and has no growing response.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum q_n\sin(n\pi x/l)$, with $q_n$ as above. A point force at a mode’s node does not excite that mode.
exercises.pattern: Point-source delta → sample the mode shape to obtain modal force → independent forced ODEs → check nodes and resonance.
exercises.pitfall: The point force is a total force; its source includes $\delta(x-x_0)$. Do not distribute it uniformly along the string.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: End-force driving of a fixed–free rod
exercises.question: A uniform slender rod of length $l$ has one fixed end and a sustained force $f(t)=A\sin\omega t$ at the other. Starting at rest in equilibrium, find its forced longitudinal motion.
exercises.idea: The force acts at a boundary, not throughout the rod. Weak projection onto fixed–free modes retains the endpoint-force term.
exercises.hint: Take $x=0$ fixed and positive tensile force at $x=l$: $YSu_x(l,t)=A\sin\omega t$. Half-integer sine modes have endpoint value $(-1)^n$.
exercises.solution:
Introduce material parameters $Y,\rho,S$, with $c^2=Y/\rho$. The full problem is
$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\quad u(0,t)=0,\quad YSu_x(l,t)=A\sin\omega t,\quad u(x,0)=u_t(x,0)=0.$$
Use $X_n=\sin k_nx$, $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$, and $\Omega_n=ck_n$. Multiply the PDE by $X_n$ and integrate by parts twice. Since $X_n'(l)=0$, the boundary contribution is $c^2u_x(l,t)X_n(l)$. Divide by the squared norm $l/2$:
$$q_n''+\Omega_n^2q_n=G_n\sin\omega t,\qquad G_n=\frac{2A(-1)^n}{\rho Sl}.$$
Off resonance,
$$q_n=\frac{G_n}{\Omega_n^2-\omega^2}\left(\sin\omega t-\frac\omega{\Omega_n}\sin\Omega_nt\right),\quad u=\sum_{n\ge0}q_n\sin k_nx.$$
If $\omega=\Omega_N$, replace that modal term by $G_N[\sin\Omega_Nt-\Omega_Nt\cos\Omega_Nt]/(2\Omega_N^2)$.
Interpret this expansion initially as an energy or weak solution. Each basis function has zero derivative at the right endpoint, but one cannot differentiate the series there term by term to reject the nonhomogeneous end force. The integration by parts has retained the actual boundary flux. Alternatively, set $u=w+x f(t)/(YS)$ to make the boundary homogeneous before expanding; this gives the same solution.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum_{n\ge0}q_n\sin[(n+1/2)\pi x/l]$, with modal force $G_n=2A(-1)^n/(\rho Sl)$ and the nonresonant or resonant response above.
exercises.pattern: Boundary forcing → write the stress boundary first → weak projection or boundary lifting → endpoint values give modal forces → check resonance.
exercises.pitfall: Do not put $f(t)$ into a uniform source inside the rod. Do not differentiate the modal series term by term at the endpoint without justification.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A point impulse on an infinite string
exercises.question: An infinite uniform string starts at rest in equilibrium. At $t=0$, a total impulse $I$ acts at $x=x_0$. Find its motion.
exercises.idea: A point impulse creates delta initial velocity. Integrate it with d’Alembert’s formula.
exercises.hint: $u(x,0)=0$ and $u_t(x,0)=(I/\rho)\delta(x-x_0)$.
exercises.solution:
Let linear density be $\rho$, tension $T$, and wave speed $c=\sqrt{T/\rho}$. The impulse–momentum relation gives $\rho u_t(x,0)=I\delta(x-x_0)$. D’Alembert’s solution on the full line is
$$u(x,t)=\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}\frac I\rho\delta(s-x_0)ds.$$
For $|x-x_0|<ct$, the interval contains the impact point and the displacement is $I/(2\rho c)$. For $|x-x_0|>ct$, it is zero. Thus
$$u(x,t)=\frac{I}{2\rho c}H(ct-|x-x_0|).$$
Two wavefronts travel left and right at speed $c$. At a wavefront, symmetric regularization gives the half value. The initial velocity and equation hold in the distributional sense.
exercises.pattern: Point impulse → delta initial velocity → integrate over the d’Alembert interval → decide whether the impact point is inside the characteristic interval.
exercises.pitfall: This is an initial-velocity pulse, not a delta initial displacement. Do not simply add two shifted deltas.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A general half-infinite string with prescribed end displacement
exercises.question: Fully solve textbook equation (3.1.161): $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=0$ for $x>0,t>0$, $u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$, $u_t(x,0)=v(x)$, and $u(0,t)=g(t)$.
exercises.idea: Superpose the initial-data response and boundary driving. Oddly extend the initial data for a homogeneous boundary; the prescribed end displacement travels along a characteristic with a delay.
exercises.hint: Let $\varphi_o,v_o$ be the odd extensions. The boundary response is $H(t-x/c)g(t-x/c)$.
exercises.solution:
1. Define $\varphi_o(s)=\varphi(s)$ for $s>0$ and $-\varphi(-s)$ for $s<0$. Extend $v_o$ as the odd extension of the initial velocity in the same way. D’Alembert’s formula gives
$$u_1=\frac{\varphi_o(x-ct)+\varphi_o(x+ct)}2+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v_o(s)ds.$$
This satisfies the given initial data and $u_1(0,t)=0$.
2. The zero-initial-data boundary response is $u_2=H(t-x/c)g(t-x/c)$. A boundary signal takes time $x/c$ to reach position $x$.
3. Add them: $u=u_1+u_2$. Explicitly, for $x>ct$,
$$u=\frac{\varphi(x-ct)+\varphi(x+ct)}2+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v(s)ds;$$
for $0<x<ct$,
$$u=\frac{\varphi(x+ct)-\varphi(ct-x)}2+\frac1{2c}\int_{ct-x}^{ct+x}v(s)ds+g(t-x/c).$$
A continuous classical solution requires $g(0)=\varphi(0)$. Greater smoothness also requires $g'(0)=v(0)$ and further compatibility. Without compatibility, the formula still describes a weak solution with a jump along a characteristic.
exercises.answer: $u=\tfrac12[\varphi_o(x-ct)+\varphi_o(x+ct)]+(2c)^{-1}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v_o(s)ds+H(t-x/c)g(t-x/c)$.
exercises.pattern: Nonhomogeneous displacement at a half-line boundary → superpose → odd extension reflects initial data → delayed propagation carries the boundary signal → check corner compatibility.
exercises.pitfall: After reflection, the initial-velocity integral begins at $ct-x$. Do not use the positive-half-line original function unchanged across zero.
exercises.verification: PDF page 142 / printed page 133 was read to confirm that (3.1.161) combines nonzero initial data with a prescribed end displacement. Independently derived using d’Alembert’s formula and delayed propagation.

exercises.title: A sinusoidal end force on a half-infinite string
exercises.question: A half-infinite uniform string has zero initial displacement and velocity. A periodic force $f(t)=A\sin\omega t$ acts at its end $x=0$. Find its motion.
exercises.idea: End force prescribes a Neumann condition. The time derivative of a right-traveling wave is proportional to that force.
exercises.hint: Define positive force in the positive $u$ direction. The left-end condition is $-Tu_x(0,t)=f(t)$.
exercises.solution:
Let $c=\sqrt{T/\rho}$ and exclude an incoming wave from infinity. Before arrival the displacement is zero; afterward write $u=w(s)$ with $s=t-x/c$. Then $u_x=-w'(s)/c$, so the end-force condition gives
$$\frac Tc w'(t)=A\sin\omega t,\quad w(0)=0.$$
Integration gives $w(t)=Ac[1-\cos\omega t]/(T\omega)$. Therefore
$$u(x,t)=\frac{Ac}{T\omega}[1-\cos\omega(t-x/c)]H(t-x/c)=\frac{A}{\rho c\omega}[1-\cos\omega(t-x/c)]H(t-x/c).$$
Because $w(0)=w'(0)=0$, no extra displacement or velocity delta appears at the wavefront. Substitution into the left-end derivative gives the required force. Reversing the positive force convention reverses the overall sign.
exercises.answer: $u=A[1-\cos\omega(t-x/c)]H(t-x/c)/(\rho c\omega)$, for $\omega>0$ and left-end positive-force condition $-Tu_x=f$.
exercises.pattern: Half-line end force → choose an outgoing wave → relate force to the wave derivative → integrate once → include the arrival step function.
exercises.pitfall: The end force $A\sin\omega t$ is not the end displacement. Writing $A\sin\omega(t-x/c)$ directly confuses both the boundary condition and the units.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Heating of a current-carrying rod
exercises.question: A uniform metal rod of length $l$ carries a steady current $I$. It has cross-section $S$, density $\rho$, specific heat $c$, thermal conductivity $k$, and electrical resistivity $r$. The lateral surface is insulated. Its ends have $u(0,t)=0,u(l,t)=u_0$, and initially $u(x,0)=u_0x/l$. (1) Derive the complete problem. (2) Find temperature by separation.
exercises.idea: A segment releases Joule heat at rate $I^2r\,dx/S$. First find the steady state including the uniform source, then expand the decaying remainder.
exercises.hint: $\kappa=k/(\rho c)$, $q=I^2r/(\rho cS^2)$, and the steady state is $U=u_0x/l+q x(l-x)/(2\kappa)$.
exercises.solution:
Heat balance on a short segment is
$$\rho cS u_tdx=kS u_{xx}dx+I^2\frac{r\,dx}S.$$
Hence $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}+q$, where $\kappa=k/(\rho c)$ and $q=I^2r/(\rho cS^2)$, together with the given endpoint and initial conditions.
The steady state satisfies $\kappa U''+q=0$, yielding $U=u_0x/l+q x(l-x)/(2\kappa)$. Set $w=u-U$. Then $w_t=\kappa w_{xx}$ with zero endpoints and $w(x,0)=-q x(l-x)/(2\kappa)$.
Using $\frac2l\int_0^l x(l-x)\sin(n\pi x/l)dx=4l^2[1-(-1)^n]/(n^3\pi^3)$ gives
$$u=\frac{u_0x}l+\frac q{2\kappa}x(l-x)-\frac{4ql^2}{\kappa\pi^3}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\sin[(2m+1)\pi x/l]}{(2m+1)^3}e^{-\kappa[(2m+1)\pi/l]^2t}.$$
At $t=0$, the series cancels the parabolic term. As $t\to\infty$, the temperature approaches the Joule-heated parabolic steady state.
exercises.answer: $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}+q$, with $\kappa=k/(\rho c)$ and $q=I^2r/(\rho cS^2)$. The solution is $u=U+$ the negative decaying odd-sine series above.
exercises.pattern: Heat equation with source and nonzero boundaries → use heat balance to fix source units → find the steady state → homogenize → project the initial difference.
exercises.pitfall: $r$ is resistivity. Resistance per unit length is $r/S$, so dividing the heating rate by heat capacity makes the normalized source contain $S^2$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Hydration heat in concrete
exercises.question: After concrete is poured, it releases hydration heat. The stored hydration-energy density $Q$ satisfies $dQ/dt=-\beta Q$. The specific heat is $c$, density $\rho$, and initial stored energy density $Q_0$. Derive the heat equation.
exercises.idea: The rate at which stored energy decreases is the heat-release rate. The source is $-Q_t$, not $Q$.
exercises.hint: $Q(t)=Q_0e^{-\beta t}$, so the released power density is $\beta Q_0e^{-\beta t}$.
exercises.solution:
Solving the stored-energy equation gives $Q=Q_0e^{-\beta t}$. Heat released per unit volume per unit time is $q=-dQ/dt=\beta Q_0e^{-\beta t}$. With uniform thermal conductivity $k$, local heat conservation is
$$\rho c u_t=k\Delta u+\beta Q_0e^{-\beta t},$$
or
$$u_t=\frac{k}{\rho c}\Delta u+\frac{\beta Q_0}{\rho c}e^{-\beta t}.$$
If the initial energy density $Q_0$ varies with position, use $Q_0(\mathbf x)$. Geometry, initial temperature, and boundary conditions are not given, so the equation can be formulated but temperature cannot be uniquely determined.
exercises.answer: $\rho c u_t=k\Delta u+\beta Q_0e^{-\beta t}$.
exercises.pattern: Solve for the stored reaction energy → take its negative time derivative as the heat source → divide by volumetric heat capacity.
exercises.pitfall: $Q$ is remaining energy density; $\beta Q$ is power density. The heat source is positive.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Boundary conditions for a sunlit blackened sphere
exercises.question: A metal sphere of radius $r_0$ has a blackened surface and is exposed to sunlight. Solar heat-flux intensity is $q_0$ and ambient temperature is $\theta$. Determine the boundary condition.
exercises.idea: Balance energy flux locally on the sphere: absorbed sunlight and heat loss to the environment determine normal conduction. State the heat-transfer model explicitly.
exercises.hint: The local absorbed flux is $q_0\max(0,\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf s)$, where $\mathbf s$ points toward the sun.
exercises.solution:
Let $u$ be temperature, $k$ thermal conductivity, $\mathbf n$ the outward surface normal, and $\mathbf s$ point toward the sun. Outward conductive heat flux is $-k\partial_nu$. A blackened surface approximately absorbs all incident radiation, giving absorbed power per area $q_0\max(0,\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf s)$. Local energy balance gives
$$-k\partial_nu=R(u,\theta)-q_0\max(0,\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf s),\quad r=r_0.$$
Here $R$ is the net heat-loss model. With the Newton cooling law commonly used in this course, $R=h(u-\theta)$, where $h$ is the surface heat-transfer coefficient. Thus
$$k u_r+h(u-\theta)=q_0\max(0,\cos\alpha).$$
For ideal blackbody radiation without convection, use $R=\sigma_{\rm SB}(u^4-\theta^4)$ with temperatures in kelvin:
$$k u_r+\sigma_{\rm SB}(u^4-\theta^4)=q_0\max(0,\cos\alpha).$$
The question supplies neither $h$ nor a definite heat-loss law, so one cannot uniquely choose a linear or radiative boundary. State the chosen model. The shaded side receives zero sunlight. Even though metal conducts well, setting the local incident flux to $q_0$ everywhere on the sphere requires an additional approximation.
exercises.answer: In general, $-k\partial_nu=R(u,\theta)-q_0\max(0,\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf s)$. Newton cooling gives $ku_r+h(u-\theta)=q_0\max(0,\cos\alpha)$; blackbody radiation replaces the cooling term by $\sigma_{\rm SB}(u^4-\theta^4)$.
exercises.pattern: Surface heating → define the outward normal → balance absorption and heat loss against conduction → project the sunlight angle → state the heat-transfer law.
exercises.pitfall: The incident flux includes $\cos\alpha$ and is zero on the shaded side. Ambient temperature is not automatically the surface temperature.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the original question by flux balance. The missing heat-loss law is handled by explicitly stating different physical assumptions; no unique model is claimed.

exercises.title: Heat decay in a rod with one fixed-temperature and one insulated end
exercises.question: A uniform slender rod of length $l$ has an insulated lateral surface. Its end $x=0$ is held at zero temperature and its end $x=l$ is insulated. Initial temperature is $x(l-x)$. (1) Give the complete problem. (2) Find the time-dependent temperature by separation.
exercises.idea: Zero temperature at one end and insulation at the other give mixed boundaries and half-integer sine modes. Textbook questions 4 and 5 are identical, so their solutions must agree.
exercises.hint: The spatial wavenumbers are $(n+1/2)\pi/l$. Keep both integration-by-parts contributions when projecting the polynomial.
exercises.solution:
Let $\kappa=k/(\rho c)>0$. The full problem is $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$ for $0<x<l,t>0$, $u(0,t)=0,u_x(l,t)=0$, and $u(x,0)=x(l-x)$.
Separation gives $X_n=\sin k_nx$, $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$, and time factor $e^{-\kappa k_n^2t}$. The squared norm is $l/2$. Integrating by parts twice gives
$$A_n=\frac2l\int_0^l x(l-x)\sin k_nx\,dx=\frac4{lk_n^3}-\frac{2(-1)^n}{k_n^2}.$$
Therefore
$$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left[\frac4{lk_n^3}-\frac{2(-1)^n}{k_n^2}\right]\sin k_nx\,e^{-\kappa k_n^2t}.$$
The initial temperature has derivative $-l$ at the right end, so the initial data and insulated boundary are incompatible at that corner. The heat equation smooths for $t>0$; recover the initial data by interior or L² limits. All modes eventually decay to zero because the left end remains at zero temperature.
exercises.answer: $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$, $u(0,t)=0,u_x(l,t)=0$, and initial temperature $x(l-x)$. $u=\sum_{n\ge0}[4/(lk_n^3)-2(-1)^n/k_n^2]\sin k_nx\,e^{-\kappa k_n^2t}$ with $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$.
exercises.pattern: Mixed thermal boundaries → half-integer sine modes → project the initial temperature → multiply each mode by its diffusion decay factor.
exercises.pitfall: Insulation means $u_x(l,t)=0$, not $u(l,t)=0$. Textbook question 5 repeats question 4; do not invent a different question.
exercises.verification: Questions 4 and 5 on printed page 150 were compared word for word and confirmed identical. Coefficients and thermal decay rates were independently checked.
exercises.errata: Textbook questions 4 and 5 repeat the same problem. Both original numbers are retained to avoid appearing to omit a question. The solution explains the initial–boundary incompatibility at the right endpoint.

The heat equation smooths for $t>0$; recover the initial data by interior or L² limits. All modes eventually decay to zero because the left end remains at zero temperature.
exercises.answer: $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$, $u(0,t)=0,u_x(l,t)=0$, and initial temperature $x(l-x)$. $u=\sum_{n\ge0}[4/(lk_n^3)-2(-1)^n/k_n^2]\sin k_nx\,e^{-\kappa k_n^2t}$ with $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$.
exercises.pattern: Mixed thermal boundaries → half-integer sine modes → project the initial temperature → multiply each mode by its diffusion decay factor.
exercises.pitfall: Insulation means $u_x(l,t)=0$, not $u(l,t)=0$. Textbook question 5 repeats question 4; do not invent a different question.
exercises.verification: Questions 4 and 5 on printed page 150 were compared word for word and confirmed identical. Coefficients and thermal decay rates were independently checked.
exercises.errata: This repeats question 4 in the same section. The original number is retained; the eigenfunction expansion and compatibility discussion are the same.

exercises.title: A zero-end-temperature rod with its modes already given
exercises.question: A uniform rod of length $l$ has an insulated lateral surface and both ends held at zero temperature. Its initial temperature is $3\sin(\pi x/l)+2\sin(3\pi x/l)$. (1) Formulate the problem. (2) Solve by separation.
exercises.idea: The initial temperature is already a sum of two eigenmodes, so no projection integrals are needed.
exercises.hint: The decay rates of the first and third modes are in ratio $1:9$.
exercises.solution:
The complete problem is $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$, $u(0,t)=u(l,t)=0$, with the given initial temperature and $\kappa=k/(\rho c)$. Each fixed-end mode $\sin(n\pi x/l)$ gains time factor $e^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2t/l^2}$. Thus
$$u(x,t)=3e^{-\kappa\pi^2t/l^2}\sin\frac{\pi x}l+2e^{-9\kappa\pi^2t/l^2}\sin\frac{3\pi x}l.$$
At $t=0$ this recovers the initial temperature, and both endpoint values stay zero. Differentiation verifies the heat equation term by term. The third mode decays faster, so the first dominates at long times.
exercises.answer: $u=3e^{-\kappa\pi^2t/l^2}\sin(\pi x/l)+2e^{-9\kappa\pi^2t/l^2}\sin(3\pi x/l)$.
exercises.pattern: Initial temperature already given as eigenfunctions → keep their coefficients → attach the appropriate decay factor to each mode.
exercises.pitfall: The third mode’s exponent is multiplied by $9$, not $3$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Positive temperature feedback and a critical rod length
exercises.question: A uniform slender rod of length $l$ has an insulated lateral surface and zero temperature at both ends. Heat generated per unit length per unit time is proportional to the local temperature, with coefficient $\beta>0$. Initial temperature is $\varphi(x)$. (1) Find the temperature. (2) Find the critical length above which temperature growth is possible.
exercises.idea: A source proportional to temperature subtracts a constant from each diffusion decay rate. The smallest spatial eigenvalue determines the onset of growth.
exercises.hint: Let heat capacity per unit length be $C=\rho cS$ and conduction parameter $K=kS$. Set $\gamma=\beta/C$, $\kappa=K/C$.
exercises.solution:
Heat conservation per unit length is $C u_t=K u_{xx}+\beta u$. Thus $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}+\gamma u$, where $\kappa=K/C$ and $\gamma=\beta/C$, with zero endpoint temperatures and initial data $\varphi$.
Expand $\varphi=\sum a_n\sin(n\pi x/l)$, where $a_n=(2/l)\int_0^l\varphi\sin(n\pi x/l)dx$. Each mode satisfies $q_n'=[\gamma-\kappa(n\pi/l)^2]q_n$, so
$$u=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n e^{[\gamma-\kappa(n\pi/l)^2]t}\sin\frac{n\pi x}l.$$
The first mode’s growth rate becomes positive first. Hence
$$l_c=\pi\sqrt{\kappa/\gamma}=\pi\sqrt{K/\beta}=\pi\sqrt{kS/\beta}.$$
For $l<l_c$, all modes decay. At $l=l_c$, the first mode is constant in time. For $l>l_c$, growing modes exist. Actual growth also requires the initial data to have a nonzero projection onto at least one growing mode. For example, nonzero nonnegative initial temperature has $a_1>0$. Zero initial data, or data orthogonal to every growing mode, are exceptions. If a course handout instead defines $\beta$ as the already-normalized coefficient in $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}+\beta u$, the corresponding notation is $l_c=\pi\sqrt{\kappa/\beta}$.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum a_ne^{[\gamma-\kappa(n\pi/l)^2]t}\sin(n\pi x/l)$. The critical length is $l_c=\pi\sqrt{\kappa/\gamma}$, with $\gamma=\beta/(\rho cS)$, equivalently $\pi\sqrt{kS/\beta}$.
exercises.pattern: Temperature-feedback source → normalize while retaining physical units → find modal growth rates → locate the first-mode threshold → check whether initial data excite growth.
exercises.pitfall: Do not mix heat-generation coefficients per unit length with coefficients already divided by heat capacity. A length above threshold does not make the exactly zero solution spontaneously become nonzero.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: An insulated square plate
exercises.question: A uniform square plate of side $a$ lies in the first quadrant with one corner at the origin. All four edges are insulated and its initial temperature is $\varphi(x,y)$. Find the temperature at any time.
exercises.idea: Insulation gives a double-cosine basis. Retain the $(0,0)$ mode, which carries the mean temperature.
exercises.hint: Set $\eta_0=1$, $\eta_n=2$ for $n\ge1$. Then the coefficient factor is uniformly $\eta_m\eta_n/a^2$.
exercises.solution:
The equation is $u_t=\kappa(u_{xx}+u_{yy})$, with $u_x(0,y,t)=u_x(a,y,t)=0$ and $u_y(x,0,t)=u_y(x,a,t)=0$. Define
$$C_{mn}=\frac{\eta_m\eta_n}{a^2}\int_0^a\int_0^a\varphi(x,y)\cos\frac{m\pi x}a\cos\frac{n\pi y}a\,dxdy,$$
where $m,n\ge0$, $\eta_0=1,\eta_j=2$ for $j>0$. Then
$$u=\sum_{m,n\ge0}C_{mn}e^{-\kappa\pi^2(m^2+n^2)t/a^2}\cos\frac{m\pi x}a\cos\frac{n\pi y}a.$$
The zero mode $C_{00}=a^{-2}\iint\varphi$ does not decay; every other mode does. Thus as $t\to\infty$, the temperature becomes uniform at the initial mean, consistent with heat conservation for four insulated edges.
exercises.answer: The double-cosine series is given above, with $C_{mn}=\eta_m\eta_n a^{-2}\iint\varphi\cos(m\pi x/a)\cos(n\pi y/a)$. The long-time temperature is $C_{00}$.
exercises.pattern: All edges insulated → Neumann double-cosine basis including zero frequencies → project with the correct zero/nonzero norms → mean temperature is conserved.
exercises.pitfall: Starting at $m,n=1$ loses the mean temperature and modes varying in only one direction. The initial temperature then generally cannot be recovered.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A rectangle with prescribed top-edge temperature
exercises.question: Solve $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ in $0<x<a,0<y<b$, with $u(0,y)=u(a,y)=0$, $u(x,0)=0$, and $u(x,b)=f(x)$.
exercises.idea: The two zero side values select a sine basis. The zero bottom value then selects the hyperbolic sine.
exercises.hint: Expand $f$ in a sine series on $(0,a)$.
exercises.solution:
Set $k_n=n\pi/a$. Separation gives $X_n=\sin k_nx$ and $Y_n''-k_n^2Y_n=0$. Since $Y_n(0)=0$, choose $\sinh k_ny$. Normalize its value at the top to $1$:
$$u(x,y)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\frac{\sinh k_ny}{\sinh k_nb}\sin k_nx,\qquad f_n=\frac2a\int_0^a f(s)\sin k_ns\,ds.$$
The side and bottom values hold term by term; the top reproduces $f$’s sine expansion. Every term satisfies Laplace’s equation $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. For continuity on the closed rectangle, corner compatibility requires $f(0)=f(a)=0$. Otherwise interpret the boundary data as traces or limits away from the corners.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum_{n\ge1}f_n\sinh(n\pi y/a)\sin(n\pi x/a)/\sinh(n\pi b/a)$.
exercises.pattern: Three zero edges and one prescribed edge → eigenfunctions in the homogeneous direction → a hyperbolic ratio across the rectangle → project the boundary values.
exercises.pitfall: The denominator is the hyperbolic sine evaluated at the top. Omitting this normalization gives the wrong top-edge coefficients.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: A rectangle with mixed boundaries and prescribed flux
exercises.question: Solve $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ in $0<x<a,0<y<b$, with $u(0,y)=0$, $u_x(a,y)=f(y)$, $u(x,0)=0$, and $u_y(x,b)=0$.
exercises.idea: The mixed bottom/top boundaries select half-integer sine modes. The right boundary prescribes a derivative, so normalize the derivative of the hyperbolic factor.
exercises.hint: $\mu_n=(n+1/2)\pi/b$. The right-edge derivative introduces $\mu_n\cosh(\mu_na)$.
exercises.solution:
From $Y(0)=0,Y'(b)=0$, obtain $Y_n=\sin\mu_ny$, with $\mu_n=(n+1/2)\pi/b$ for $n\ge0$. In $x$, $X_n''-\mu_n^2X_n=0$ and $X_n(0)=0$, so choose $\sinh\mu_nx$. Let
$$f_n=\frac2b\int_0^b f(s)\sin\mu_ns\,ds.$$
To make the right derivative equal the expansion of $f$, take
$$u(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n\frac{\sinh\mu_nx}{\mu_n\cosh\mu_na}\sin\mu_ny.$$
Differentiating in $x$ and setting $x=a$ cancels the normalization factor exactly. The other three homogeneous boundary conditions also hold.
exercises.answer: $u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_n\sinh(\mu_nx)\sin(\mu_ny)/[\mu_n\cosh(\mu_na)]$, with $f_n=2b^{-1}\int_0^bf\sin\mu_ns\,ds$.
exercises.pattern: Homogeneous mixed boundaries → half-integer spectrum → normalize the derivative at the nonzero-flux edge → project the boundary data.
exercises.pitfall: The right side specifies $u_x$. Its denominator must be $\mu_n\cosh\mu_na$, not $\sinh\mu_na$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Superposition for two nonzero steady boundaries
exercises.question: Inside a rectangle, $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. The boundaries are $u(0,y)=Ay(b-y)$, $u(a,y)=0$, $u(x,0)=B\sin(\pi x/a)$, and $u(x,b)=0$. Find $u$.
exercises.idea: Split by linear superposition into one problem with only the left edge nonzero and another with only the bottom edge nonzero.
exercises.hint: The sine expansion of $Ay(b-y)$ contains only odd n, with coefficients $8Ab^2/(n^3\pi^3)$.
exercises.solution:
Let $u=v+w$. Function $v$ carries only the left data $Ay(b-y)$, with zero values on the other three edges. Function $w$ carries only the bottom data $B\sin(\pi x/a)$, with zero values on the other edges.
The left-edge projection coefficients are
$$c_n=\frac2b\int_0^b Ay(b-y)\sin\frac{n\pi y}b dy=\frac{4Ab^2[1-(-1)^n]}{n^3\pi^3}.$$
Thus
$$v=\frac{8Ab^2}{\pi^3}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\sinh[(2m+1)\pi(a-x)/b]}{(2m+1)^3\sinh[(2m+1)\pi a/b]}\sin\frac{(2m+1)\pi y}b.$$
The bottom data are a single mode, giving
$$w=B\frac{\sinh[\pi(b-y)/a]}{\sinh(\pi b/a)}\sin\frac{\pi x}a.$$
Add the two parts. All four corner values are zero and compatible. On $x=0$ and $y=0$, respectively, the other part is zero, so the prescribed data are recovered.
exercises.answer: $u=v+w$, where $v$ is the left-edge odd-sine series above and $w=B\sinh[\pi(b-y)/a]\sin(\pi x/a)/\sinh(\pi b/a)$.
exercises.pattern: Several nonzero edges → split into single-edge problems → choose the appropriate orthogonal direction for each → check every edge after adding.
exercises.pitfall: Use $a-x$ for the left-driven term so it vanishes on the right. Use $b-y$ for the bottom-driven term so it vanishes on the top.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Self-adjoint form of Laguerre’s equation
exercises.question: Put Laguerre’s equation $xy''+(1-x)y'+ay=0$ in standard Sturm–Liouville form and determine its weight.
exercises.idea: Find a multiplier that combines the first and second derivatives into one total derivative.
exercises.hint: Multiply by $e^{-x}$, since $(xe^{-x})'=(1-x)e^{-x}$.
exercises.solution:
Multiplication by $e^{-x}$ gives $xe^{-x}y''+(1-x)e^{-x}y'+ae^{-x}y=0$. The first two terms combine to give
$$(xe^{-x}y')'+ae^{-x}y=0.$$
Comparing with $(py')'-qy+\lambda wy=0$, obtain $p=xe^{-x},q=0,\lambda=a,w=e^{-x}$. The usual interval is $(0,\infty)$, where the weight is positive. To study Laguerre-polynomial orthogonality, suitable regular or integrable solutions must also be chosen at zero and infinity. The differential equation alone does not determine the full boundary spectrum.
exercises.answer: $(xe^{-x}y')'+ae^{-x}y=0$, with weight $w=e^{-x}$, up to a positive constant factor.
exercises.pattern: Self-adjoint conversion → choose a multiplier satisfying $(\mu a_2)'=\mu a_1$ → identify the coefficient of the eigenvalue as the weight.
exercises.pitfall: The weight is the coefficient multiplying the eigenvalue parameter, not the derivative coefficient $xe^{-x}$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Self-adjoint form of Hermite’s equation
exercises.question: Put Hermite’s equation $y''-2xy'+2ay=0$ in standard Sturm–Liouville form and determine its weight.
exercises.idea: The first-derivative term suggests a Gaussian integrating factor.
exercises.hint: Multiply by $e^{-x^2}$, whose derivative is $-2xe^{-x^2}$.
exercises.solution:
Multiplying by $e^{-x^2}$ gives
$$e^{-x^2}y''-2xe^{-x^2}y'+2ae^{-x^2}y=0,$$
or
$$(e^{-x^2}y')'+2ae^{-x^2}y=0.$$
Take $p=e^{-x^2},q=0,\lambda=2a,w=e^{-x^2}$. If one instead insists on $\lambda=a$, use weight $2e^{-x^2}$, differing only by a positive constant. The usual interval is the full line, with inner product $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}fg\,dx$. Boundary behavior must make the integrals and boundary terms appropriate.
exercises.pattern: Integrate the first-derivative coefficient → obtain a Gaussian multiplier → form a total derivative → state the eigenvalue-parameter convention.
exercises.pitfall: Do not mix the choices λ=$2a$ and λ=$a$. A positive constant may be absorbed into the weight, but it must match the chosen parameter.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Self-adjoint form of Chebyshev’s equation
exercises.question: Put Chebyshev’s equation $(1-x^2)y''-xy'+n^2y=0$ in standard Sturm–Liouville form and determine its weight.
exercises.idea: Choose a multiplier so that the derivative of $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ matches the first-derivative term.
exercises.solution:
After multiplying by $1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$, the derivative terms are
$$\sqrt{1-x^2}y''-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}y'=(\sqrt{1-x^2}y')'.$$
Hence
$$(\sqrt{1-x^2}y')'+n^2\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=0.$$
Read off $p=\sqrt{1-x^2},q=0,\lambda=n^2,w=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$. The standard interval is $(-1,1)$, with singular endpoints. Although the weight diverges there, it is integrable. Under $x=\cos\theta$, $w\,dx$ becomes $-d\theta$, explaining the weighted orthogonality of $T_n(x)=\cos(n\theta)$.
exercises.pattern: Find an integrating factor → identify the weight → check the orthogonality weight by a trigonometric substitution.
exercises.pitfall: The weight is the inverse square root; do not interchange it with $p=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question; checked by substitution, projection coefficients, and boundary conditions.

exercises.title: Real eigenvalues and a counterexample to nonnegativity
exercises.question: Consider $(k y')'-q y+\lambda\rho y=0$ for $a<x<b$, with $\alpha_1y(a)+\alpha_2y'(a)=0$ and $\beta_1y(b)+\beta_2y'(b)=0$. The question gives nonnegative real functions $k,q,\rho$ and real boundary constants, and asks to prove: (1) all eigenvalues are real; (2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative.
exercises.idea: Use the Lagrange identity to prove reality and the energy quotient to inspect nonnegativity. The second statement lacks boundary sign conditions and is false as written.
exercises.hint: Counterexample: on $(0,1)$, take $k=\rho=1,q=0$ and $y'-y=0$ at both endpoints. The function $y=e^x$ has $\lambda=-1$.
exercises.solution:
First add the standard nondegeneracy assumptions: a regular problem needs $k>0,\rho>0$, and the two boundary coefficients at either endpoint cannot both be zero. Mere nonnegativity permits degeneracy; for example, $\rho\equiv0$ removes the parameter’s spectral meaning.
(1) Multiply the equation for eigenfunction $y$ by $\bar y$ and subtract its conjugate multiplied by $y$. Integration over $[a,b]$ gives
$$(\lambda-\bar\lambda)\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx=-[k(y'\bar y-y\bar y')]_a^b.$$
The real separated boundaries make the bracket zero at each endpoint: for Dirichlet data $y=0$; otherwise $y'$ is a real constant times $y$. The integral is strictly positive, hence $\lambda=\bar\lambda$.
(2) The original claim that all real boundary constants give nonnegative eigenvalues is false. Set $a=0,b=1,k=\rho=1,q=0$, with $y'(0)-y(0)=y'(1)-y(1)=0$. The nonzero function $y=e^x$ satisfies both boundaries and $y''-y=0$, giving $\lambda=-1<0$. All coefficient requirements in the question are met.
The correct test comes from the energy quotient:
$$\lambda=\frac{\int_a^b[k|y'|^2+q|y|^2]dx-[ky'\bar y]_a^b}{\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx}.$$
Dirichlet or Neumann boundaries eliminate the boundary term, so $\lambda\ge0$. For Robin conditions at both ends with $\alpha_2\beta_2\ne0$, the boundary contribution is
$$k(b)\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_2}|y(b)|^2-k(a)\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2}|y(a)|^2.$$
For example, adding $\alpha_1/\alpha_2\le0$ and $\beta_1/\beta_2\ge0$ ensures nonnegativity. More generally, the necessary and sufficient formulation is nonnegativity of the whole energy quadratic form. One must not discard the Robin boundaries allowed by the question just to complete a proof.
exercises.answer: (1) Eigenvalues are real under the standard nondegenerate self-adjoint assumptions. (2) The original statement is false: $y=e^x$ with $y'-y=0$ at both ends gives $\lambda=-1$. Only after adding conditions making the energy boundary contribution nonnegative can one conclude $\lambda\ge0$.
exercises.pattern: Spectral-property question → inspect the assumptions → subtract conjugates to prove reality → use the energy quotient for signs → when assumptions fail, give a concrete counterexample and a correct statement.
exercises.pitfall: Real Robin boundaries ensure self-adjointness and a real spectrum, but do not automatically ensure a nonnegative spectrum. Do not drop the boundary term after integration by parts.
exercises.verification: The equation and both boundaries were checked for $y=e^x$. The energy quotient was independently derived. The missing condition in textbook part (2) is explicitly marked.
exercises.errata: Part (2) incorrectly claims nonnegative eigenvalues for arbitrary real Robin coefficients. The solution gives a λ=−1 counterexample and sufficient energy conditions for nonnegativity.
